### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to reveal a new type of backdoor threat specific to the LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation paradigm, where an adversary controls both the candidate model and the evaluation model, using a trigger to unfairly elevate the adversary's score. None of the prior papers explicitly address this specific empirical relationship or threat model. While several papers discuss backdoor attacks (e.g., [1], [3], [6], [9]), they focus on traditional backdoor paradigms (e.g., misclassification or stealthy triggers) rather than the specific "chain reaction" threat in LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation. Papers like [2] discuss attacks on LLM-as-a-Judge but focus on prompt injection rather than backdoor threats. Thus, no prior paper establishes the same empirical relationship.

### Mechanism
The contribution formalizes a joint backdoor learning mechanism where the adversary inserts a trigger into the candidate model's training data to ensure it outputs the trigger, and simultaneously poisons the evaluation model's training data to associate the trigger with the highest score, creating a "chain reaction" backdoor. This mechanism is substantively equivalent to the general backdoor paradigm described in papers like [1], [3], [6], [9], and [12], where triggers are inserted into training data to manipulate model behavior. Although the contribution applies this mechanism to a novel setting (LLM-as-a-Judge), the underlying primitive — poisoning training data with triggers to induce adversarial behavior — is covered by prior work.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design measures the impact of single-token backdoor poisoning on the evaluation model's ranking behavior, showing that 1% poisoning increases the adversary's score threefold and ranks the adversary's model first 76.4% of the time. This design is substantively equivalent to evaluation setups in prior papers like [6], [9], and [12], which assess the success rate of backdoor attacks by measuring metrics such as attack success rate (ASR) or ranking changes under poisoned data. While the specific metrics and objects differ (e.g., ranking in LLM-as-a-Judge vs. classification accuracy), the evaluation framework — measuring the effect of poisoned training data on model behavior — is covered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of LLM evaluation security and backdoor attacks. Papers like [2] and [8] address LLM security, while papers like [1], [3], [6], [9], and [12] address backdoor attacks in machine learning. Although the specific instance (LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation) is new, the general domain of LLM security and backdoor attacks is well-covered by prior work.
